label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
reason: formatting, assistant talk or a placeholder
output:
Here's a draft. I wrote it to be read out loud, so the sentences are short enough for Denise to get through without tripping. Where you see [your name], put in whatever Nana calls you.

---

Dear Nana,

Denise is reading this to you, so hi Denise, thank you for doing this, and please don't do a voice. If she does a voice, Nana, that's not how I sound.

First thing: I'm sorry I'm not there. I'm on call for the whole week, and I asked everyone I could think of to swap with me and nobody would. I know you're going to say it's fine. Everybody has told me it's fine. I know it's fine. I still wanted to be sitting at that table with you tonight, so this is the next best thing, which is me talking at you for a few minutes while you can't interrupt. I know that's rare.

I started this letter about six times this week and closed the laptop every time, because I'd get a few lines in and get choked up. So if Denise's voice cracks, that's on me. I passed it along.

I've been thinking about that kitchen. Fifty-one years in that house, and you raised half the family in that one room. I only got the summers, but they were the best part of my whole childhood. I remember the little TV on the counter and the Expos or the Jays on late, and you letting me stay up for it as long as I dried the dishes. It took me about twenty years to figure out that I got paid in baseball and you got a very cheap dishwasher. I'd do it again. I want that on the record.

I remember you teaching me crib when I was about seven, and never once letting me win. Not one time. Not even a little. Eight years of that, and then when I was fifteen I finally skunked you, and you didn't say a word. You went and made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I still don't know if those were a prize or an apology, and I've decided not to ask.

And the back steps. You out there at six in the morning with your tea, and me coming out half asleep, and you not saying one word until the cup was empty. Nobody explained the rule to me. I just picked it up. I think that's where I learned you can sit next to someone and not talk and it still counts. I use that more than you'd guess. I work with a lot of people who could stand to learn it.

When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card. It said it was for pizza, because I looked thin on the computer. I want you to know I bought the pizza. I'd like to say that's the only reason I'm not still thin, but I think it was more than one pizza.

And then there's the pager. Last Christmas it went off in the middle of dinner, and you asked whether the internet was broken again and whether I'd fixed it. Now every time I'm on call you ask me, "Did anything break?" I have been doing this job for a long time, and that is still the best summary of it I've ever heard. Most of the time the answer is yes, and I fix it, and nobody notices. That's the whole job. You're the only one who ever asks.

So, as it happens, I am on call this week, and something might break. If it does, I'll fix it. Please don't ask Denise about it.

Now the real reason I wanted to write this. I know leaving that house is a big thing, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't. Grandpa Walt is in that house too, and so is every Sunday dinner and every kid who ever got sent to sit on the back steps. But I've been thinking about it all week, and here's what I keep landing on: the house is you. The kitchen was warm because you were standing in it. The back steps were good because you were sitting on them. None of that is in the wallpaper. It goes where you go. You're not leaving it behind. You're taking it with you, in a couple of boxes and a very good coat.

And you picked this. I want to say that part clearly, because I'm so proud of you for it. Nobody talked you into it and nobody pushed. You looked at your life at 88 and decided what you wanted next, and then you went and did it yourself. Most people can't do that at 38. I'm 34 and I can't decide what to have for lunch.

I've looked at the pictures of Elmwood Terrace. Second floor, and your window looks out at a big maple tree and the parking lot. I'm told that's where all the real news happens, so you'll know everything about everyone in that building by Thursday. And they have a crib league. I read that line twice. Nana, those people have no idea what's about to happen to them. Please go easy on them for at least the first week. Let them have a hand or two. You can start showing no mercy once they've gotten comfortable.

I know Tuesdays with the church ladies aren't going anywhere, either. They'll just have to learn to drive a little farther.

I also owe you a confession about the move. Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I asked for the crib board. I know that looks like I got the short end. But I think I got the better deal, because a cuckoo clock doesn't keep score, and the board does. It's the one thing in the house I know for certain will end up with my name on the losing side. That's worth more to me than any clock.

I'm coming up the weekend of December 5, as soon as this rotation is over. I'm not coming to the house on Kathleen Street, I'm coming to Elmwood. I'll bring the board, you can show me where you want the table, and you can deal the first hand. The first game at the new place. And I know you're not going to let me win. Please don't start now.

I love you, Nana. Have your tea on the steps one more time tomorrow morning. Take as long as you like with the cup.

See you on the 5th.

Love,
[your name]

---

A couple of things to check before Denise reads it:

- **The things I made up.** The "Sunday dinners" line, the "good coat," and the teasing about knowing everyone's business at Elmwood are my guesses at her. Cut anything that doesn't sound like Nana.
- **"Eight years of that."** That's just 7 to 15. If you really did play regularly the whole time, it's fine. If not, change it to "years of that."
- **The back steps line at the end.** I wrote it as if she'll be on them the morning of the 21st. If the movers or the schedule make that unlikely, you could change it to "one more cup of tea on the steps if you get the chance."
- **Length.** It's about 1,000 words, which reads aloud in around 6 or 7 minutes. If you want it longer, the best places to add are another summer memory or a story about Grandpa Walt. If you'd rather keep it moving, it also holds up with the Elmwood paragraph trimmed.

If you tell me more about how she talks, I can adjust the voice so it sounds even more like you.
